title: Economic growth is becoming less reliably job-creating as Bangladesh’s sectoral employment elasticities shift
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 111458, Structural Shift in Job Creation: Evidence from Bangladesh
geography: Bangladesh, with comparative Okun’s-law analysis involving six other Asian countries and sectoral employment-elasticity estimates for 2003-2024

observations.period: Bangladesh and six other Asian countries; growth–employment relationship

denominator.unit: Asian countries in the comparative Okun's-law analysis

okun_evidence.value: evidence supporting a conventional Okun's-law relationship is weaker for Bangladesh than for the other selected countries

modeling.value: three autoregressive distributed-lag specifications are used: dynamic difference, Hodrick-Prescott gap, and Baxter-King gap models

growth_job_gap.value: aggregate growth is a less reliable proxy for employment creation in Bangladesh

household_route.value: when growth and job creation decouple, household room depends more on sector, job quality, participation, and wage conversion than on headline GDP growth

observations.method: Time-series autoregressive distributed-lag estimates using three specifications to test the growth–employment relationship across Bangladesh and six Asian comparison countries.
observations.uncertainty: Macro time-series results depend on sample period, filters, specification, structural breaks, data quality, and employment measurement; they do not identify a single causal mechanism or worker-level distribution.
observations.subgroup: Bangladesh workers and sectors, comparison-country labor markets, formal and informal workers, women and men, rural and urban households, and workers moving across sectors.
observations.counterinterpretation: A weak aggregate Okun relationship can reflect labor-force participation, productivity, hours, migration, informality, measurement, or sectoral composition rather than a complete absence of job creation.

observations.period: Bangladesh; employment elasticity of growth across 2003-2010 and 2016-2024

denominator.unit: Bangladesh employment-elasticity periods analyzed in the paper

agriculture.value: employment elasticity in agriculture increased from 0.29 in 2003-2010 to 0.98 in 2016-2024

industry.value: employment elasticity in industry declined from 0.84 to -0.04 over the compared periods

structural_shift.value: growth has not moved uniformly toward increasingly job-rich industrialization; the sectoral employment response has changed direction

quality_boundary.value: elasticity measures the employment response to growth, not job quality, wage adequacy, stability, bargaining power, or household security

observations.method: Sectoral employment-elasticity estimates across three Bangladesh periods, with comparisons of agriculture, industry, and services.
observations.uncertainty: The reported period comparisons are sensitive to sector definitions, employment data, macro shocks, productivity, labor substitution, and the choice of subperiods; they do not establish that growth caused the sectoral movements.
observations.subgroup: Agricultural workers, industrial workers, manufacturing workers, rural-to-urban migrants, women entering or leaving sectors, and households dependent on sectoral earnings.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower industry elasticity can coexist with productivity or wage gains, and a higher agricultural elasticity can reflect low-quality or seasonal work rather than inclusive structural transformation.

strongest_subsectors.value: accommodation and food services and transportation and storage show the strongest employment elasticity

manufacturing.value: manufacturing employment elasticity turns negative and performs worst among the analyzed sectors

consumer_route.value: growth may create jobs in service activities tied to movement and consumption while reducing the employment response in manufacturing

policy_question.value: employment-enhancing growth requires sector choice and job-quality attention, not only aggregate growth targets

observations.method: Granular sector and subsector analysis of employment elasticity within Bangladesh's industry and service categories.
observations.uncertainty: Subsector elasticities are descriptive macro estimates and do not reveal whether new jobs are formal, durable, adequately paid, safe, geographically accessible, or equally available to women and disadvantaged groups.
observations.subgroup: Manufacturing workers, accommodation and food-service workers, transport and storage workers, consumers, migrants, firms, and households exposed to changing sectoral demand.
observations.counterinterpretation: Service-sector job creation may be lower-productivity or precarious, while manufacturing's negative elasticity may reflect capital deepening, trade exposure, automation, or reclassification rather than net welfare loss.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank record and metadata for the Bangladesh growth and jobs study.
Bibliographic record and abstract for the Okun-law comparison, period elasticities, sector results, and subsector findings.
World Bank reproducibility package and study metadata.

boundary: This record adds a growth-to-job-quality and sectoral-conversion mechanism. It is macro time-series evidence, not a causal worker-level evaluation, a measure of realized household welfare, or proof that services are better than manufacturing or that aggregate growth has no employment benefit.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF, document page, abstract record, and reproducibility metadata were reviewed for the seven-country Okun-law comparison, three model specifications, Bangladesh employment elasticities, agriculture/industry changes, service and manufacturing subsectors, 2003-2024 periods, and quality and causal boundaries.
